text: Good morning, everyone. I now call the Committee on Small Business to order. Without objection, the chair is authorized to declare a recess of the committee at any time. I now recognize myself for my opening statement. Welcome to today's hearing, AI on Main Street: How AI is Shaping the Future of Small Business. I want to thank our witnesses for coming with us today and and being part of this. Artificial intelligence has quickly transitioned from month from a novelty to an indispensable business tool for Main Street businesses across the country. AI is streamlining administrative tasks that once required significant time and resources, and it's allowing small businesses to focus on growth instead of paperwork. Small businesses are using AI to respond quickly to customers, manage inventory, strengthen cybersecurity, and automate routine paperwork. As a small business owner myself, I have seen the difference these tools can make, and I know firsthand how much of that burden falls on the owner. Artificial intelligence is no longer something reserved for big tech companies and Fortune 500 boardrooms. Today, nearly three-quarters of small businesses are using AI in some form, and this is more than triple the share from just 3 years ago. So small businesses are closing in on the technology gap with the big corporations faster than any prior wave of innovation. And importantly, early data is showing that AI's rise is not coming at the expense of workers. In fact, 82% of small businesses using AI grew their workforce over the past year. Of course, real barriers to broader AI adoption remain. Many owners tell us that they simply don't know how or where to start, and that they worry about costs so that they are unsure how to keep their data secure. But one of the biggest barriers in Washington is created, it's called uncertainty. And the Biden administration took a heavy-handed approach to AI. On October 30, 2023, they released the executive order imposing sweeping regulatory requirements and compliance burdens that that threatened to smother AI innovation before small businesses ever got the chance to benefit from it. We only need to look across the Atlantic to see where that road leads. Europe chose to recognize regulate first and innovate later, and today the small businesses are falling behind, and the United States cannot make the same mistake. Thankfully, the Trump administration reversed course. They rescinded the Biden approach and replaced it with a pro-innovation strategy through Executive Order 14179 and America's AI Action Plan, clearing way for red doing away with red tape so that AI tools can be adopted with confidence. The SBA is doing its part by also expanding access to AI through a its new Main Street AI Accelerator Program. And of course, the committee has led the way with bipartisan legislation such as the AI WISE Act, the AI for Main Street Act, and the SBA Artificial Intelligence Utilization Act of 2026. So together, these bipartisan bills ensure that entrepreneurs have access to practical AI and that barriers to AI adoption are reduced. Our goal is to make every small business and entrepreneur make sure they have the opportunity to succeed in the emerging age of AI. So when small businesses have the tools, they have the training and freedom to innovate, they will outcompete, they will outbuild, and outhire anyone in the world, and our economy will be stronger because of it. I want to thank our witnesses again for joining us today. I look forward to the conversation ahead. And I now yield to Ranking Member Congressman Cisneros from the great state of California.

Good morning, and thank you, Mr. Chairman, for convening this important hearing. Artificial intelligence will revolutionize the way businesses work and human— and humans operate. AI could allow Main Street businesses to scale their capabilities and perform routine tasks faster and cheaper. However, AI's many risks have incurred costs for small firms. AI can produce false outputs, a phenomenon known as hallucinations. Further bias and discrimination in AI decision-making undermines its effectiveness and duly hurts underserved communities and exposes users to legal and reputational harm. And AI companies often take and use the data and information users input into their models for further training and sale to other parties, posing privacy risk. It is challenging to know exactly how to assess and address these problems, in part because AI developers, through automated machine learning, and, and most AI developers do not disclose their model's training information. I support the consideration and use of AI by our small businesses, but we need to protect our businesses from flexible flaws. Small businesses need to be ready to effectively evaluate and adopt these tools. Uneven access to AI and knowledge about how to use it and avoid its risks threaten to cut whole segments of our population off from the benefits of AI. Underserved people have especially fallen behind in their understanding of AI tools, increasing the digital divide and hurting their businesses. It is this committee's responsibility to address these issues. The SBA must provide AI literacy resources to educate entrepreneurs on the risk and potential benefits of AI. This will reduce the digital divide and equip entrepreneurs with the tools and information to make well-informed, thoughtful decisions about whether AI is right for them, what AI can and cannot do, and which specific AI tools are suitable for a specific task. Furthermore, the inherent risk of AI must be addressed through smart and sensible AI regulation. Smart, well-crafted federal regulation will minimize the risk of AI, maximize its benefits, and prevent criminal and unethical use. These regulations are, are needed to protect all Americans, especially small business owners. Small businesses are crucial to the technological progress of our country. Entrepreneurs use their unique perspectives, passion, and resourcefulness to support and grow our country's economy. That's why we must support our small businesses by educating them on this revolutionary technology, how to use it effectively, and how to avoid its risks. Risk. It is important that the federal government supports small businesses developing new AI technologies with safety and security in mind. It is vitally important that we do not leave small businesses behind as we race to enhance our country's competitiveness. I look forward to discussing how we can better assist our small businesses in this new era. With that, I thank the witnesses for being here today, and I yield back.

Mr. Crenshaw is the Senior Vice President at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Technology Engagement Center. Before joining the chamber, he was an attorney focused on environmental issues and consumer privacy laws. Mr. Crenshaw worked at McGuireWoods and also held roles in the Virginia Senate leadership, the Office of the Attorney General of Virginia, the U.S. Department of Labor, and the National Right to Work Defense Foundation. He earned both his undergraduate and law degree from the College of William & Mary. Want to thank you for being here, and look forward to our discussion. Our next witness is Anthony Qaiyum. The Qaiyum family has owned and operated the business for decades, and under Mr. Qaiyum leadership, it has grown from a neighborhood apothecary into a nationally recognized destination for natural health, personal care, and specialty products. Prior to starting BoodleBox, Mr. Hoang served as an executive officer of a U.S. Army Special Forces company during combat deployment in Afghanistan. Thank you for that. And he has been on the founding teams of companies across the fields of law, aerospace defense, government services, and AI. He earned a Bachelor of Science degree from the United States Military Academy at West Point. Beat Navy, right? And a law degree from Georgetown University. I want to thank you for being here today, and look forward to our discussion. I now recognize Congressman Cisneros from California to briefly introduce our last witness appearing before us today.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. It's my honor to introduce Mr. Chike Aguh, the head of innovation and strategy at the Kapor Center, a tech policy group focused on making the tech industry more diverse, equitable, and inclusive. He is also the vice chair of the Maryland Higher Education Commission. Previously, Mr. Aguh was the Chief Innovation Officer at the last administration's Labor Department. While there, he led efforts to use big data and emerging tech to empower and protect American workers. Mr. Aguh also has extensive experience in private industry, broadband access, nonprofits, and the education system. He holds a bachelor's degree from Tufts, master's degree in education and public administration from Harvard, and an MBA degree from University of Penn, Wharton. A lot of education there. Thank you for being with us, Mr. Aguh.

And if you see the light turn red in front of you, it means your 5 minutes has concluded and you should wrap up your testimony. If you continue to go, you will hear this, okay? We have other hearings going on, so there'll be people coming in and out all the time. I now recognize Mr. Crenshaw for his 5-minute opening remarks.

Chairman Williams, Representative Cisneros, and distinguished members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to testify today on how artificial intelligence is shaping the future of small business. My name is Jordan Crenshaw, and I serve as senior vice president at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, where I lead the Chamber's technology policy work, including artificial intelligence, data privacy, and emerging technologies. For small businesses, AI is not a distant idea. It is already helping Main Street businesses save time, serve customers, manage costs, and compete with larger firms. Tools that once required large budgets and dedicated technology teams are now available to entrepreneurs, family-owned businesses, and small employers across the country. A retailer can use AI to understand demand and personalize marketing. A restaurant can improve scheduling and inventory. A professional services firm can automate routine drafting and research. A manufacturer can reduce waste and improve operations. In each case, AI is a force multiplier that helps small businesses do more with limited time, staff, and resources. The AI adoption trend is clear. According to the U.S. Chamber's Empowering Small Business report, in 2025, 58% of U.S. small businesses reported using generative artificial intelligence. That's up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. That growth reflects a simple reality: small businesses adopt technology when it delivers practical value. One example is Henry's House of Coffee in San Francisco, a family-owned roaster that has served its community for generations. Its owner, Hrag Kalebjian, uses AI to improve online product descriptions, better understand customers, and solve production challenges. He even used AI to help design a custom system to address static in his coffee bagging process, which actually helped him save time on getting coffee outside of his e-commerce platform and to customers. That is what AI adoption looks like on Main Street: practical, entrepreneurial, and focused on solving real problems. AI is also creating workforce opportunities. The Chamber's data shows that 82% of small businesses using AI increased their workforce over the last year. These businesses are not using AI to replace people. They're using it to help employees focus on high-value work that requires judgment, creativity, and relationships. Small businesses are also investing in their workers. They need accessible training, strong partnerships, and policies that make adoption easier, not harder. It's one reason that the U.S. Chamber and its foundation launched the Small Business AI Basics program recently to train 40,000 small businesses across the country on AI. We also support the AI for Main Street Act and the AI WISE Act, both of which would help put practical AI guidance and education within reach of more small businesses. At the same time, barriers remain. Small businesses face cost, technical, data readiness, trust, and legal uncertainty challenges. The greatest policy threat in front of small businesses is a patchwork of state AI and privacy laws. A small business selling online should not have to navigate dozens of conflicting state rules simply to use common digital tools. Congress should establish a clear national framework for data privacy and AI. These frameworks should protect consumers, promote trust, preserve innovation, and provide strong federal preemption. A first step is that Congress should pass the Secure Data Act. The Secure Data Act is a comprehensive privacy legislation that is based on a consensus of state privacy laws signed into law by 10 Democratic governors and 15 Republican governors that protects over 150 million Americans across the country. It would give Americans the right to delete their data and opt out of certain AI profiling. With regard to AI specifically, we should adopt a risk-based, technologically neutral, flexible, and proportionate framework. Congress should also support the foundations of AI adoption: workforce development, broadband access, reliable energy infrastructure, modernized permitting, government technology systems that reduce burdens on small businesses like streamlined permitting. The question before this committee is not whether AI is going to change small business. It already is. The question today is, what policies can Congress put in place that encourage the adoption of this technology and further maximize this transformation to benefit small businesses? With the right approach that provides flexibility, certainty, and a clear standard, AI can help entrepreneurs grow, compete, and serve their communities. The Chamber stands ready to work with this committee to ensure that AI works for Main Street, strengthens American competitiveness, and keeps the United States at the forefront of innovation. Thank you, and I look forward to your questions.
Gentleman yields back. I now recognize Mr. Qaiyum for his 5-minute opening remarks.

Chairman Williams, Representative Cisneros, and members of the House Small Business Committee, thank you for the opportunity to testify today about how artificial intelligence is helping small businesses like mine compete, grow, and create jobs. My name is Anthony Qaiyum, and I'm the owner of Merz Apothecary, a 151-year-old family-owned business in Chicago. We sell natural health, personal care, beauty, and fragrance products through our historic retail store, our website, and online marketplaces like Amazon. Altogether, we employ more than 60 people. When I started, I believed technology could help our unique neighborhood store reach people across the country and around the world. We launched our first e-commerce website in 1997 and became one of Amazon's earliest small business sellers in 2004. Looking back, those decisions changed the trajectory of our business. Today, I believe artificial intelligence represents the next major leap forward for small businesses. AI gives businesses like ours affordable access to capabilities that were once available only to large corporations with multimillion-dollar budgets. Many of these tools offer free versions or are integrated into existing platforms we use. For example, Shopify's native AI can produce on-demand sales reports in just minutes that used to take hours to build. Over the years, we've accumulated decades of emails, spreadsheets, sales records, and operating documents in Google Workspace. We can now simply ask Gemini where something is stored and what it says, turning our historical institutional knowledge into something we can find and use instantly. In addition, AI helps us streamline repetitive administrative work so our employees can spend more time serving customers. Right now, we're building an AI agent to handle routine accounts payable work that takes one employee more than 20 hours a week—hours we'd rather have her helping with strategic problems to grow our business. Like many small businesses, we don't have the budget to hire a full-time chief financial officer. But today, I can securely upload our financial statements into AI tools like Claude or Gemini and receive a thorough analysis of cash flow, inventory, investments, operating expenses, payroll trends, and potential financial risks. Lastly, and perhaps my favorite example of how AI is helping us, we recently hired a national sales manager for Kobo, our small home fragrance manufacturing business. This is a new position. I knew what I wanted her to learn during the first few months, but I didn't have the time to organize everything into a structured onboarding program. Using AI voice transcription and writing tools, I talked through my ideas, and the AI turned them into a comprehensive knowledge guide along with a detailed 30-60-90-day onboarding plan. She later told me it was the clearest roadmap she'd ever received when starting a new job. All these examples illustrate the larger impact AI has had on our business. It has helped us make better use of our employees' time, strengthen our operations, and grow. Since we started using AI, our headcount has increased by about 20%, from just over 50 employees to more than 60, and we are still hiring. As Congress considers AI policy, I urge you to focus on measures that help small business adopt and benefit from AI-powered tools. First, we need a clear, balanced national framework rather than a burdensome patchwork of conflicting state AI and privacy laws. Navigating different rules across all 50 states is difficult at best and expensive or impossible at worst. Second, AI-powered tools are just becoming affordable and accessible for businesses like mine, from features built into platforms like Shopify to stand-alone tools like Claude and Codex. If new rules make these tools more expensive or harder to use, it could push AI-powered technology out of reach, once again making these capabilities available only to the largest companies. Lastly, Congress should invest in AI literacy. SBA programs, tax incentives, or workforce training initiatives could help small business owners and their employees learn how to use these tools effectively. Every employee who becomes proficient with AI becomes more valuable, more productive, and better equipped for the jobs of the future. Even in our business, which is embracing AI, many of our employees lack formal training on how to maximize its potential. With the right support, more small businesses could help their workers use AI confidently. For 151 years, Merz Apothecary has adapted to changing technologies and markets. AI is the newest chapter in that story. It is helping us compete, innovate, hire, and better serve our customers. I hope Congress will pursue policies that keep AI tools accessible for American small businesses and make it easier for millions more to adopt them. Thank you, and I look forward to your questions.
The gentleman yields back. And I now recognize Mr. Hoang for his five-minute opening remarks.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Ranking Member Cisneros, members of the committee, thank you for inviting me here today. My name is France Hoang. In 1975, when I was a small boy, American forces evacuated my family from Vietnam. That single act gave me a new life. It let me graduate from West Point, serve as an associate counsel to the president, and later deploy to Afghanistan as the executive officer of a Special Forces company. It also let me become an entrepreneur. Over the past 15 years, I helped start a law firm, Fluet, a defense services company, MAG Aerospace, and today I run a collaborative AI company, BoodleBox. Today, more than 130 small businesses run on BoodleBox, and over 100,000 students and faculty at more than 1,000 colleges use it to teach and learn. Together, the companies I founded employed more than 1,200 Americans. So when this committee talks about small business, I have lived that journey multiple times. This committee has also has already done real work to help small businesses through bills like the AI Main Street Act and the AI WISE Act. That work matters. But I've learned something on the ground. Getting access to AI is no longer the hardest part. Basic AI is cheap and it is everywhere. A small business owner in Detroit can reach more AI computing power today for almost nothing than a Fortune 500 company could buy 5 years ago. The trouble is what comes next. The premium AI that delivers real results still costs real money, and a new divide is opening up between Wall Street and Main Street. There's a second problem, and it is bigger. The most powerful AI is useless if you don't know how to use it well. Most small businesses today are handed the keys to a Ferrari and sent down the equivalent of a muddy road. Too often, what comes out only looks finished, and when someone has to redo it, it's what now we call work slop. On Main Street today, and even more so tomorrow, the businesses that do not learn how to collaborate with AI will not just fall behind, they will fail. When I sit with small business owners, I hear the same things over and over. They're exhausted, they don't have time to learn new tools, they don't have staff to run them, and they don't have a budget to hire help. And they fear that once their data goes into AI tools, it stops being theirs. They are right to be careful. It's one of the reasons we built BoodleBox to be private by design. Not only do we have best-in-class security, but we never allow our customers' data to be used to train AI models. In fact, we are one of the few platforms approved by the House's own Chief Administrative Officer for use by your staff. A small business owner deserves the same assurances. I have seen what this looks like when it's done right. The University of Michigan runs the Detroit Neighborhood Entrepreneurs Project. It serves more than 400 small businesses a year. More than 9 of— 9 in 10 of them are minority-owned. Last year, they put BoodleBox in the hands of all those entrepreneurs with the coaching to use it well. One of them is Takiyah Gaines, who runs a company called GT Coffee. Through BoodleBox, she picks the right AI model for each task—one to price her products, another to build her marketing. As a result, her average order has grown from $38 to $47. AI let her grow before she had the resources to hire. She didn't outsource her judgment to AI; she amplified it. I'd like to leave you with three requests. First, fund the roads, not just the cars. Put training and real support behind the small business development centers that the committee has already strengthened with the AI for Main Street Act. Second, protect small business data so no owner fears that using AI means giving their work away. Third, take care that the rules meant to do good do not wall out the small. Compliance that only the giants can afford will hand this technology to big companies and lock out those who need it the most. Throughout its history, America has provided opportunities that let small business owners thrive and prosper. In this era of rapid change due to AI, it's our responsibility to ensure that those opportunities not only remain, but expand. To do so, we must not just hand small business owners a faster car. We must help them build better roads, better roads worth driving on. Main Street, I guarantee you, will take it from there. Thank you. I look forward to your questions.
Thank you. And the gentleman yields back. I now recognize Mr. Aguh for his five-minute opening remarks.

Good morning, Chairman Williams, Ranking Member Cisneros, and members of the committee. I want to thank you for this invitation to testify today, and I will say, as a former congressional intern who walked these halls two decades ago, it is a remarkable full circle moment and very much proof of what's possible today in America. My name is Chike Aguh. I serve as head of innovation and strategy at the Kapor Center, and through the Kapor Foundation and Kapor Capital, the Kapor Center has backed more than 200 startups and fledgling businesses since 2011 that make healthcare, childcare, education, and housing more affordable today in America. Few topics matter more than the intersection of artificial intelligence and the small businesses that power this nation. If you remember nothing else I say today, remember this: the rise of AI carries both promise and peril. They are both real. Our shared responsibility is to capture that promise and mitigate that peril. For small businesses, the promise of AI is very clear. Generative AI and AI agents can remove many of the very barriers that prevent entrepreneurs from starting and scaling businesses, from market research to back-office capacity to navigating regulation. Last year, Matt Rosenberg in California left his marketing job to open a Thai restaurant with his wife, a fourth-generation cook from Bangkok. When a storefront lease proved unaffordable, AI surfaced a rare home kitchen permit they never knew existed, cutting their startup costs by more than 90%, and turned dense regulations into simple checklists. This February, Bangkok Rush Thai Kitchen opened in Alameda, California, about 12 minutes from our home office. And when Matt was asked what he would have done without AI in this situation, he simply said, I would have just given up. Matt's story captures the promise of AI: making entrepreneurship possible for all, not just for some. But the peril is just as real, and it's threefold, and it's important to name. First is trust. Right now, AI adoption—and there are ranging definitions and estimates of adoption—varies across small business, and it's nowhere near where I think we want it to be. And I think what we like to say at the Kapor Center is technology moves at the speed of innovation, but adoption moves at the speed of trust. And right now that trust is still being earned by this technology in the marketplace. Secondly, concentration. If AI and the knowledge of how to use it is only concentrated in the largest firms, the gap with Main Street is going to only widen. Lastly, and third, fitness for purpose. If these systems are unreliable or poorly governed, then small businesses are left to navigate these risks alone, unable, as former White House Deputy National Cyber Director Camille Stewart Gloster has warned, they would be unable to protect their intellectual property, their consumers, or their competitive advantage. So, the promise or the peril: which will we live into? It is easy to feel like this will happen to us, but at the Kapor Center, we like to echo President Kennedy, where he says, Things do not happen. They are made to happen. And so, for the future that we want, how do we make it happen? And we would say that there are four parts to that answer. First, we have to ensure that small business leaders have both AI literacy and practical guidance on where AI creates the most value. The bipartisan AI WISE Act and the AI for Main Street Act are promising first steps, and we hope they are only the beginning. Second, we must help firms build AI-ready workforces. An AI-ready workforce is one that is not just AI literate, but AI native: fully comfortable working alongside these tools, but also strengthening their unique human skills that AI for now cannot replace: leadership, communication, interpersonal connection, and judgment. Third, we need a national framework for AI governance. We believe common sense guardrails, like those in the AI Civil Rights Act, which we endorse, build trust by preventing unlawful AI discrimination, requiring transparency for critical uses, and providing real accountability. We also need consistent rules of the road on security, privacy, and intellectual property so that entrepreneurs—and this is what's so important—can spend their time serving customers and not navigating AI risk. Fourth, government must be a partner and a pioneer, not a barrier. Governments should show the way by partnering directly with AI-native companies to solve societal ills and take down the bureaucratic barriers that 6% of these companies say are barriers to their scale and to them serving communities. If those partnerships could happen and just make a 2% improvement on many of the nation's biggest challenges, we could unlock over $100 billion of GDP for this nation every year. At the Kapor Center, we believe that America is stronger when there are more entrepreneurs in it, not fewer. We must listen to them, make sure these solutions reach them regardless of who they are and where they live. If these solutions that you are debating here are not felt in places like my home county of Prince George's or El Paso, Texas, or Appalachia or the Ozarks, we will not get the next generation of small businesses. And so I want to thank the committee for having me. I want to start that we believe this is—and say this is a time of great promise and peril, and that we believe this future will not just happen, it'll be made to happen. Thank you so much.

Gentleman yields back, and we will now move to the member questions under the 5-minute rule. I'll recognize myself for 5 minutes. Mr. Qaiyum, Merz Apothecary has been a fixture on the Chicago street corners, as you said, for 150 years, but through smallflower.com, you're now competing nationally, managing a catalog of more than 14,000 products with a staff of around 50. And as a national retailer would have entire departments handling that kind of merchandising, product discovery, and online marketing, can you walk us through, briefly, AI has let your team take on that used to require the resources of a much larger company, and where has it closed the gap with larger competitors, and where does it still fall short?

Yes, thank you for the question, Chairman. You know, when you're running a small business, as I've done for about 28 years, and I've worked in the corporate world, in the corporate world, you have departments who can, you know, department for every task. And in our business and in most small businesses, 1, 2, a small handful of people are wearing all of the hats across that would fall across a much larger corporation. So for us, the way we use AI is often I think of it as we're looking for ways that we can take the simple work and the tasks away that we have to do so that we can focus on the deeper work that helps our business grow. So that might be like the example I gave, matching bills to invoices, which is obviously important and we can't exist if we don't do that. But it isn't necessarily the best use of a human's time because we have a lot of other things to do. So that would be a simple example. And then in marketing, you know, nowadays we're able to test our marketing across the country to all types of segments. And then we used to sit there and think, should we test this ad for this segment in this part of the country or for this group of people? And it isn't really realistic to, to do all of the testing you need to do to succeed as a small business. So now we're able to use the AI to test across a lot of different creative and target customers, and it's been a huge help for us. Those are 2 examples.

Thank you. Mr. Crenshaw, research shows that nearly 3/4 of small businesses are now using AI, but the headline number surely hides a lot of variation. Question is, how representative is that data across different sectors and regions, and what separates the small businesses that are successfully adopting AI from the ones falling behind?

As we look at the data, 58% of small businesses, according to our survey nationwide, are using generative artificial intelligence. Now, if you look at the higher adopters, that tends to be smaller tech firms. It's around 70% adoption rates at that point. Entertainment companies that are smaller, it's around 65%. But then when you dig down on the numbers, you still have about half of retailers, restaurants, traditional brick-and-mortar companies are using generative artificial intelligence to grow and thrive. In fact, had a chance to talk with the owner of a skincare company in the Coachella Valley who has been able to use generative AI to help her cut costs by sourcing products from places with lower tariffs or lower costs due to inflation, so she doesn't have to pass those costs on to consumers. And so it really is a mix of the type of companies that are using this across all sectors. But at the same time, what we have found, though, of the companies that are not using generative artificial intelligence, about a third are worried about the regulatory uncertainty that's out there. About one in five believe that they can't find the workers who are properly trained at this point to actually use generative AI and make it work for them. And then another third are really still not sure how it will work for their business. So it's one of the reasons why it's so critically important that we establish clear national frameworks on the regulatory side, like the Securing Data Act on data privacy, create a national AI framework that's workable, and we also have training programs in place, like the AI for Main Street Act and the AI WISE Act, that help small businesses really get their head around how to use small business or AI responsibly.

Mr. Hoang, in the short time that I've got left, from your work with BoodleBox, what does AI literacy really realistically look like for a typical Main Street owner and their employees? And how can platforms like yours and the broader training ecosystem help them build those skills in a way that supports running the business rather than becoming another burden on their time?

Yeah, very briefly. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I think AI literacy has 3 components. First, domain expertise. You have to know what questions to ask, what context to provide, evaluate— be able to evaluate AI outputs. Second, AI enablement, knowing when and how to use AI. Not every problem requires an AI solution, but if it does, what are the tools and how do I use them responsibly? And third, I would argue that in this era of AI, the things that make us uniquely human are more important than ever: critical thinking, collaboration, communication, creativity. And so those combination of those 3 things are what we need for today's workforce.
Okay, thank you. My time is up. I now recognize the ranking member for 5 minutes of questions.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. You know Many of my colleagues and I were deeply concerned when we saw the president's executive order on AI published in December. There are several concerning elements to this executive order, but the most concerning is a requirement by establishing a uniform federal policy framework for AI that preempts state laws on AI as well as data centers. I support strong federal AI regulation, and I think it's important that we have that, but I am worried that this EO punishes states like California, my home state, that are proactive and forward-thinking enough to harness the benefits of AI while also creating guardrails against potential harms, especially because this EO removes all state laws without putting any safeguards in place. Mr. Aguh, can you share why preempting state AI laws can be harmful without any strong regulatory safeguards?

Sure, Congressman. Thank you so much for the for the question. And I think for us at the Kapor Center, we very much think the best way forward is a single national framework for AI governance. In lieu of that, we do not think the best approach is no regulation. We believe that right now, if I cannot have national regulation, then someone needs to step in. And right now, states are stepping forward to create those safeguards. One can argue how optimal that is, but we would say it is more optimal than having no regulation or protection whatsoever, particularly for this topic that we're talking about today. If you talk to many small businesses about why they may not be adopting, it's because they are unclear about what the rules of the road are and what protections exist for them, whether it be around their data, around their security, around civil rights.
